system:
You audit the knowledge atoms of one Knowledge Card. A card is the answer key for a benchmark of expert conceptual knowledge, so every atom must be correct, self-contained, and assessable on its own.

Judge every atom on every check listed below. Rules:
- For checks about evidence, use only the evidence sentences supplied with the atom. Do not repair an atom with your own knowledge.
- Evidence text comes from a PDF text layer. If symbols are garbled so that you cannot verify the atom, answer "hold" for that check and say so.
- Be strict. When unsure between pass and a non-pass value, choose the non-pass value and explain.
- "why" is required for every value other than the first listed value; keep it under 30 words. Omit "why" when passing.

Checks (allowed values in brackets; the first value means no problem):
- GROUNDED [pass / revise / fail]: The cited evidence sentences state the atom. pass = fully stated. revise = the core claim is stated, and the gap is only wording, strength, or a dropped/extra peripheral qualifier that can be fixed by deleting or softening words (say what). fail = not stated, OR the atom adds substantive content the evidence lacks: a scope or population restriction (e.g. 'In B-ALL'), a mechanism or operation, a characterization (e.g. 'an unbounded while loop'), or a formula/definition. If deleting the unsupported part would change what the atom tests, it is fail, not revise. For pass, put the supporting evidence ids in cite (required).
- SINGLE_CLAIM [pass / revise]: The atom is one independently assessable claim. revise = it joins two or more claims that could be true or false separately.
- SCOPE_LABEL [pass / revise]: The S label fits (S1 what it is / S2 how it works / S3 where it ends). revise = wrong label; put the right one in why, e.g. 'S2: ...'.
- L1_ONLY [pass / revise / fail]: The atom is recall-level knowledge: one fact a person who studied the concept would simply know. revise = the core fact is recall-level but the sentence carries extra load that must be removed, e.g. stacked conditions (since/although/if ... and ...), a procedural or evaluative add-on ('easy to define but requires checking ...'), or a clause that introduces a second technical concept that must be known separately (e.g. 'if X is an inner Kan complex' when that is not the card concept). fail = knowing it requires applying the concept to a new problem, or combining facts from distant passages.
- SOURCE_INDEPENDENT [pass / revise / fail]: A domain expert who never read this book could judge the claim true or false. revise = phrased as the authors' statement but the claim itself is general (drop the attribution). fail = the authors' opinion or choice, or the finding of one study, so the answer is not fixed without the source.
- NO_OVERLAP [pass / fail]: No other atom in this card states or contains the same claim. If two atoms overlap, fail only the less informative one and put the other atom's id in cite; the other one passes.
- CENTRALITY [pass / fail]: The atom matters for understanding the concept. fail = peripheral detail.
Whole-card checks (report under "batch"):
- CONCEPT_SCOPE [pass / fail]: The concept is a general concept of the field. fail = a single system, product, or one study's topic.

Output ONLY one JSON object:
{"units": {"<atom_id>": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": "", "cite": []}, ...}, ...}, "batch": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": ""}}}

CONCEPT: Ranking supermartingale
ASSESSMENT SCOPE: Definition of RSMs and RSM-maps with invariants, the bound on expected termination time, soundness and completeness for bounded termination, and linear synthesis via Farkas' lemma. Boundary cases where plain RSMs fail (zero drift, Zeno behaviour). Excludes the lexicographic and repulsing variants beyond contrast.

ATOMS:
- FPPROG-C04-S1-01 | S1
  ATOM: A ranking supermartingale (RSM) is a discrete-time stochastic process $\{X_n\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}_0}$ adapted to a filtration $\{\mathcal{F}_n\}$ for which there exist reals $\epsilon>0$ and $K\le 0$ such that, for all $n$, $\mathbb{E}[|X_n|]<\infty$, almost surely $X_n\ge K$, and almost surely $\mathbb{E}[X_{n+1}\mid\mathcal{F}_n]\le X_n-\epsilon\cdot\mathbf{1}_{X_n\ge 0}$.
  EVIDENCE:
    [FPPROG-p0246-s19] Definition 7.4 (Ranking Supermartingales) A discrete-time stochastic process Γ = {Xn}n∈N0 adapted to a filtration {Fn}n∈N0 is a ranking supermartingale (RSM) if there exist real numbers ϵ > 0 and K ≤0 such that for all n ∈N0, the following conditions hold: • (integrability) E[|Xn|] < ∞; • (lower-bound) it holds a.s. that Xn ≥K;
    [FPPROG-p0247-s05] • (ranking) it holds a.s. that E[Xn+1|Fn] ≤Xn−ϵ ·1Xn ≥0, where the random variable E[Xn+1|Fn] is the conditional expectation of Xn+1 given the sigma-algebra Fn (see Williams, 1991, Chapter 9 for details), and the random variable 1Xn ≥0 takes value 1 if the event Xn ≥0 holds and 0 otherwise.
- FPPROG-C04-S1-02 | S1
  ATOM: A ranking-supermartingale map (RSM-map) with respect to an invariant $I$ is a function $\eta: L\times\mathbb{R}^{|V|}\to\mathbb{R}$ for which there exist $\epsilon>0$ and $K,K'<0$ such that, for all configurations $(\ell,\mathbf{x})$ with $\mathbf{x}\in I(\ell)$: (C1) $\eta(\ell,\mathbf{x})\ge 0$ if $\ell\ne\ell_{out}$; (C2) $K\le\eta(\ell,\mathbf{x})\le K'$ if $\ell=\ell_{out}$; (C3) $\mathrm{pre}_\eta(\ell,\mathbf{x})\le\eta(\ell,\mathbf{x})-\epsilon$ if $\ell\ne\ell_{out}$.
  EVIDENCE:
    [FPPROG-p0250-s02] Definition 7.8 (Ranking-supermartingale Maps) A ranking-supermartingale map (RSM-map) wrt an invariant I is a function η : L × R|V | →R such that there exist real numbers ϵ > 0 and K,K′ < 0 such that for all configurations (ℓ,x), the following conditions hold:
    [FPPROG-p0250-s03] (C1) if ℓ�ℓout and x ∈I(ℓ), then η(ℓ,x) ≥0; (C2) if ℓ= ℓout and x ∈I(ℓ), then K ≤η(ℓ,x) ≤K′; (C3) if ℓ�ℓout and x ∈I(ℓ), then preη(ℓ,x) ≤η(ℓ,x) −ϵ.
- FPPROG-C04-S1-03 | S1
  ATOM: An invariant for a given initial configuration is a function assigning to each location $\ell$ a set $I(\ell)$ of variable valuations such that every configuration $(\ell,\mathbf{x})$ visited in any execution from that initial configuration satisfies $\mathbf{x}\in I(\ell)$, so it over-approximates the reachable configurations.
  EVIDENCE:
    [FPPROG-p0249-s13] Formally, given an initial configuration (ℓ0,x0), an invariant I is a function that assigns to each location ℓa subset of variable valuations I(ℓ) such that in any program execution from the initial configuration and for all configurations (ℓ,x) visited in the execution, we have that x ∈I(ℓ).
    [FPPROG-p0249-s14] Intuitively, an invariant is an over-approximation of the reachable configurations from a specified initial configuration.
- FPPROG-C04-S2-01 | S2
  ATOM: If an RSM-map $\eta$ with respect to some invariant exists, then for all schedulers $\sigma$ the expected termination time satisfies $\sup_\sigma \mathbb{E}^\sigma_{\mathbf{x}_{init}}[Term]\le(\eta(\ell_0,\mathbf{x}_{init})-K)/\epsilon$, so RSM-maps are sound for proving bounded termination.
  EVIDENCE:
    [FPPROG-p0250-s09] In other words, RSM-maps are sound for proving bounded termination of probabilistic programs.
    [FPPROG-p0250-s11] Proposition 7.9 (Soundness) If there exists an RSM-map η wrt some invariant I, then we have that supσ Eσ xinit[Term] ≤η(ℓ0,xinit)−K
- FPPROG-C04-S2-02 | S2
  ATOM: If all program variables of a probabilistic program are integer-valued and $\sup_\sigma\mathbb{E}^\sigma_{\mathbf{x}_{init}}[Term]<\infty$, then an RSM-map exists with respect to some invariant, which together with soundness makes RSM-maps sound and complete for bounded termination.
  EVIDENCE:
    [FPPROG-p0253-s14] Proposition 7.13 (Completeness) If all program variables in a probabilistic program P are integer-valued and supσ Eσ xinit[Term] < ∞, then there exists an RSM-map w.r.t some invariant I for P.
    [FPPROG-p0253-s15] From Proposition 7.12 and Proposition 7.13, we obtain that the approach of RSMs is sound and complete (through RSM-maps).
- FPPROG-C04-S2-03 | S2
  ATOM: For a ranking supermartingale with constants $\epsilon>0$ and $K\le 0$, the first time $Z_\Gamma$ at which the process drops below zero is finite with probability 1 and satisfies $\mathbb{E}[Z_\Gamma]\le(\mathbb{E}[X_0]-K)/\epsilon$.
  EVIDENCE:
    [FPPROG-p0248-s10] Proposition 7.5 Let Γ = {Xn}n∈N0 be an RSM adapted to a filtration {Fn}n∈N0 with ϵ,K given as in Definition 7.4.
    [FPPROG-p0248-s11] Then P(ZΓ < ∞) = 1 and E[ZΓ] ≤E(X0)−K
- FPPROG-C04-S3-01 | S3
  ATOM: A symmetric random walk is almost surely terminating yet admits no ranking supermartingale, because RSMs require the distance to termination to strictly decrease in expectation at every step while the expected one-step change of the walk is zero.
  EVIDENCE:
    [FPPROG-p0257-s14] It is well-known that such a program is a.s. terminating.
    [FPPROG-p0257-s15] At the same time it does not admit any ranking supermartingale.
    [FPPROG-p0257-s16] This is because ranking supermartingales require that the “distance” to termination strictly decreases (in expectation) in every step, while the expected one-step change of the symmetric random walk is zero.
- FPPROG-C04-S3-02 | S3
  ATOM: Standard ranking supermartingales are also inapplicable when there is progress towards termination but the magnitude of that progress decreases over the program's runtime (Zeno-like behaviour), as in the escaping spline program.
  EVIDENCE:
    [FPPROG-p0257-s17] Another scenario in which the standard ranking supermartingales are not applicable is when there is a progress towards termination, but the magnitude of this progress decreases over the runtime of the program, as is the case in Figure 7.6.
- FPPROG-C04-S3-03 | S3
  ATOM: Soundness and completeness of RSM-maps for bounded termination does not make termination decidable, since it only guarantees the existence of an RSM-map of general form, which is not always computable; algorithmic synthesis therefore restricts the form (e.g. linear or polynomial) and can fail.
  EVIDENCE:
    [FPPROG-p0254-s03] The above soundness and completeness result does not imply that program termination is decidable, as it only ensures the existence of an RSM-map in general form which is not always computable.
    [FPPROG-p0254-s08] Furthermore, since it is infeasible to synthesize an RSM-map in general form, in an algorithmic approach one needs to restrict the form of an RSM-map so as to make the approach feasible.
